t.1.116.1: Then Pāṇḍu, on the mountain in the great forest, rejoiced as he beheld those five handsome sons, protected by the strength of his own arms.
t.1.116.2: Once, in the season of Madhu and Mādhava, when the forests were in full bloom, a time that bewilders all beings, the king wandered through the forest together with his wife.
t.1.116.4: Beholding the forest, adorned with varied pools of water and with lotus ponds, love was born in the heart of Pāṇḍu.
t.1.116.3: With palāśas, tilakas, mangoes, campakas and pāribhadrakas, and with many other trees rich in an abundance of fruits and flowers.
t.1.116.5: As he roamed there like an immortal, his heart filled with delight, Mādrī alone followed him, wearing a beautiful garment.
t.1.116.6: But as he gazed upon her, young and in the prime of life, clad in a thin garment, his desire swelled like a fire that has sprung up in a thicket.
t.1.116.8: Then the king seized her by force as she was alone in a secluded place, though he was held back by the queen, who struggled against him with all her strength.
t.1.116.7: Seeing the lotus-eyed woman, his equal, alone in that secluded place, the king, overpowered by the force of desire, could not restrain that passion.
t.1.116.9: But he, his whole self overcome by desire, did not heed that curse, and approached Mādrī for the act of union as if by force.
t.1.116.10: Fallen under the sway of Manmatha, to the ending of his own life, the Kauravya cast aside the fear born of the curse and went in to his beloved by force.
t.1.116.11: His understanding, as he was wholly given over to desire, was bewildered by Time itself; having churned up the whole host of his senses, it perished together with his reason.
t.1.116.12: Having united with that wife of his, O joy of the Kurus, Pāṇḍu, whose soul was supremely devoted to dharma, was joined with the law of time.
t.1.116.13: Then Mādrī, embracing the king, whose consciousness had departed, let out a cry born of grief, again and again, most piteously.
t.1.116.14: Then Kuntī with her sons, and the two Pāṇḍavas, the sons of Mādrī, came together to the place where the king lay in that state.
t.1.116.15: Then, O king, the distressed Mādrī spoke these words to Kuntī: "Come here alone; let the children stay right there."
t.1.116.16: Hearing those words of hers, she held the boys back right there, and crying out, "I am undone!", she rushed to the spot at once.
t.1.116.17: Seeing Pāṇḍu and Mādrī lying on the surface of the earth, Kuntī, her limbs overcome with grief, lamented, deeply afflicted.
t.1.116.18: Though you were always guarded by me, O hero, and were ever self-controlled, how could you transgress, knowing the curse of the forest-dweller?
t.1.116.19: Surely, Mādrī, the lord of the people was to be protected by you! How then could you, of all people, have tempted the king in a lonely place?
t.1.116.20: How did delight arise in him, who was always wretched and ever brooding on that curse, when he came upon you in a secluded place?
t.1.116.21: Blessed are you, O Bāhlīkī, and more fortunate than I, for you have seen the face of the lord of the earth filled with joy.
t.1.116.22: Though he was being enticed, and though I restrained him again and again, he did not restrain himself, wishing to make his destined fate come true.
t.1.116.24: I will follow my husband here, who has gone into the power of the dead. Rise, leave him, and protect these children.
t.1.116.23: I am the eldest lawful wife, and the foremost fruit of dharma is mine. Do not turn me back, Mādrī, from what must inevitably come to pass.
t.1.116.25: I alone shall follow my husband, who never fled from battle, for I am not yet sated with pleasures. Therefore, O elders, let this be permitted.
t.1.116.26: This best of the Bharatas came to me and perished through desire; how, then, could I cut short that desire of his in the abode of Yama?
t.1.116.28: Therefore, Kuntī, you must treat my two sons as your own sons, for this king, desiring me, has passed into the power of the dead.
t.1.116.27: Nor, noble lady, would I, living on, conduct myself toward your sons without making distinction, and in that way sin would surely touch me.
t.1.116.29: Together with the king's body, this body of mine too must be burned, well covered. Do me this kindness, noble lady.
t.1.116.31: Having spoken thus, the glorious lawful wife, the daughter of the king of the Madras, swiftly ascended the funeral fire after him, that bull among men who lay upon the pyre.
t.1.116.30: Be vigilant over the children, and be well-disposed toward me. Beyond this I see nothing else at all that needs to be enjoined.
